title: Containing blocks and stacking context
learningObjectives: Explain containing blocks and stacking context and apply the layout behaviour correctly.

understand.concept: A containing block is the reference rectangle used to calculate the size and position of certain boxes. Positioned elements commonly use a positioned ancestor as their containing block. A stacking context is an independent painting group that controls how descendants are layered relative to other contexts.
understand.whyItMatters: Unexpected offsets and z-index behaviour often come from the wrong containing block or a stacking context. Properties such as positioned elements with z-index, transforms, opacity below one, and several other features can create stacking contexts.
understand.analogy: A containing block is the reference frame for placing an item; a stacking context is a layer group whose internal order is managed together.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy is simplified; the browser uses formal formatting, containing-block, and painting rules.

explain.narrative: The outer element provides a containing block, while isolation creates a stacking context for its descendants.

examples.explanation: The outer element provides a containing block, while isolation creates a stacking context for its descendants.
examples.expectedOutput: A rendered page demonstrating the relevant CSS layout behaviour.

practise.guidedTask: Add a second overlapping sibling and investigate which stacking context controls its z-index.
practise.independentTask: Build a small layout that demonstrates this behaviour. Test long content, keyboard navigation, and narrow viewports.
hints: Inspect computed styles and layout overlays.
Change one property at a time.
Keep semantic HTML independent from visual display choices.
